q: What is OCIA? Is it the same as RCIA?
a: Yes. OCIA (Order of Christian Initiation of Adults) is the new name for RCIA (Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults). It is the way adults join the Catholic Church: a journey of learning, prayer and community that leads to baptism, confirmation and first Communion, usually at Easter.

q: Can I go to Mass before I'm baptized?
a: Yes, and you are warmly encouraged to. Anyone is welcome at Mass. Going every Sunday is one of the best ways to learn the faith.

q: What do I do at Communion if I can't receive yet?
a: You can stay in your seat and pray, or go up in line with your arms crossed over your chest. The priest or minister will give you a blessing instead of Communion. Both are completely normal.

q: Why can't I receive Communion yet?
a: Catholics believe the Eucharist is truly Jesus, and receiving it is a sign of full unity with the Church. It is the goal of your journey, which makes your first Communion at Easter something to look forward to.

q: I was baptized in another Christian church. Do I need to be baptized again?
a: Usually not. The Catholic Church recognizes baptism done with water in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit in most Christian churches. You would be received into full communion and confirmed instead. Ask your parish team, since they will confirm your situation.

A sponsor is a practicing Catholic who walks with you through the journey: they pray for you, answer questions, go to Mass with you, and stand with you at the rites. Your parish can help you find one.

q: Why do Catholics confess to a priest?
a: Jesus gave his apostles the power to forgive sins (John 20:21-23). In confession, the priest acts in the person of Christ. Hearing the words of forgiveness out loud is a real gift, and the priest can never reveal what you say.

q: When do I sit, stand and kneel at Mass?
a: Generally: stand for the opening, the Gospel, the Creed and the Our Father; sit for the readings and the homily; kneel during the Eucharistic Prayer. Customs differ a little by country, so following the people around you is perfectly fine.
Doubts and questions are a normal part of faith. Even the disciples on the road to Emmaus were confused. Bring your questions to your catechist, sponsor or priest; that is what this time is for.
